Welcome back to Dev Opportunity Radar!

This is a weekly series where I share opportunities, resources, communities, and interesting finds that I come across, with the goal of helping people discover things they might otherwise miss.

This week's edition features the Basis Fellowship, offering $50,000 to selected fellows; More Than a Hack 2027, a football analytics hackathon using real FC Barcelona match data; and the Perplexity Research Fellowship for early-career AI researchers. I'm also sharing Harness Engineering 101, a free online book that explores how AI agents work, from tool calling and context management to coding agents and retrieval-augmented generation.

If you're new to the series, you can browse previous editions, search past opportunities, and explore Community Finds, Reader Updates, and Resources Worth Checking Out on the Dev Opportunity Radar website. 📍 This Week's Opportunities

Here are a few opportunities I came across this week that I thought were worth sharing.

📌 Basis Fellowship: $50,000 for Selected Fellows

Who it's for: People working on interesting or unconventional projects, including engineers, scientists, founders, operators, and others pursuing work across different fields.

What it's about:

The Basis Fellowship offers $50,000 to selected fellows, along with access to a network of people working across different areas.

Rather than focusing on one particular industry or type of project, the fellowship is interested in people doing a wide range of work. The examples on its website include an electrical setup, a thermoelectric cloud chamber, and a neurostimulation machine. The idea is to bring together people who might be working on very different things but could benefit from finding one another.

The fellowship doesn't require equity, reporting, or restrictions on how the money is spent. Applicants can submit a portfolio and other useful information, and the application asks them to answer the questions honestly.

People from different backgrounds can apply, whether they're engineers, scientists, operators, or working in another field. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis, and an application doesn't expire if someone isn't selected immediately. Applicants can send updates when something new happens.

There's also a nomination option. If someone you nominate is selected, you receive $1,000. The website also mentions a discretionary $3,000 award for a strong submission that isn't selected.

Funding: $50,000 for selected fellows
Equity: None
Eligibility: Open to people across different fields and backgrounds
Application process: Submit a portfolio and other relevant information
Applications: Rolling basis
Deadline: No fixed deadline stated
Nomination reward: $1,000 if your nominee is selected
Additional award: A discretionary $3,000 for a strong submission that isn't selected

📌 More Than a Hack 2027: Football Analytics Hackathon

Who it's for: Football analysts, data analysts and scientists, software developers, and tech enthusiasts interested in using data and technology to understand football.

What it's about:

More Than a Hack 2027 is a football analytics hackathon organized by Mobile World Capital Barcelona, Barça Innovation Hub, and Metrica Sports. Participants work with real FC Barcelona match data to develop analytical solutions related to the game.

The hackathon has two online challenge stages, followed by an in-person final pitch at Talent Arena 2027 in Barcelona.

The Initial Challenge asks teams to estimate team possession for every frame of a football match using provided automatic tracking data and homography. Participants don't need to build player detection, identification, appearance, or calibration systems from scratch. Submissions are automatically evaluated and ranked.

The top 20 teams advance to the Innovation Challenge. In this stage, teams can explore analytical or tactical questions using a dataset of 10 professional matches. They can experiment with different approaches to analysis, modeling, interpretation, and generating insights, with specialized technical mentoring available.

The top five teams from this stage will be invited to present their projects at Talent Arena 2027 in Barcelona. Travel and accommodation expenses for the final pitch are covered. The listed prizes also include official FC Barcelona shirts, Barça Innovation Hub merchandise, and an exclusive FC Barcelona experience.

Teams must have 3 to 5 members. Teams with fewer than three members won't be eligible for the Innovation Challenge or the Final Pitch.

Registration is open until November 10, 2026. The Initial Challenge is already underway, so anyone interested should review the schedule and registration requirements before joining.

Team size: 3–5 members
Data provided: FC Barcelona match videos, automatic tracking data, and automatic event data
Registration: October 1–November 10, 2026
Initial Challenge: October 20–November 17, 2026
Innovation Challenge: November 26, 2026–January 14, 2027
Final Pitch: March 2, 2027, at Talent Arena in Barcelona

📌 Perplexity Research Fellowship: AI Research Program

Who it's for: Early-career researchers, engineers, and analysts from technical or quantitative disciplines, including fields such as physics, mathematics, cognitive science, and quantitative finance.

What it's about:

The Perplexity Research Fellowship is a full-time research program for early-career talent interested in advancing AI research. Fellows join Perplexity's R&D teams and work on research areas such as multi-agent planning, continual learning, pre-training, and human-AI interaction.

The program has two tracks:

  • Predoctoral Research Fellow: For exceptional early-career talent from technical or quantitative disciplines.
  • Postdoctoral Research Fellow: For researchers who have recently completed a PhD in a technical or quantitative discipline.

The fellowship runs for three months, with opportunities to extend the program or transition into a full-time, research-focused role. Fellows work in person alongside researchers and engineers at one of Perplexity's offices and may contribute to research publications and other research outputs.

I came across this opportunity after its priority consideration deadline had passed, but applications are still being accepted on a rolling basis until positions are filled. The priority deadline was September 30, 2026, so applications submitted now may not receive priority consideration. The November 2026 and January 2027 cohorts are listed as priority start dates, but it's worth checking the application page for current availability.

Duration: 3 months, full-time
Compensation: $180,000 annualized for predoctoral fellows and $220,000 annualized for postdoctoral fellows
Location: In person in San Francisco, Palo Alto, or New York City
Application status: Accepting applications on a rolling basis until positions are filled

📚 Resources Worth Checking Out

Not every useful find comes with an application deadline.

Here's one resource worth checking out this week.

Harness Engineering 101: A Practical Guide to Building AI Agents

Who it's for: Developers who want to understand how AI agents work, particularly those interested in LLM APIs, tool use, context management, and building coding agents.

What it's about:

Harness Engineering 101 is a free online book by Isuru Wijesiri that explores how to build AI agents from first principles.

It starts with a simple idea: an LLM provides the reasoning, while the harness is the program that manages the conversation, tools, and execution around it.

The book develops this idea across 16 chapters, using a small Python agent of approximately 300 lines as its foundation. Rather than treating agent frameworks as black boxes, it explains the problems that arise when building an agent and the changes needed to address them.

The chapters cover topics such as the agent loop, tool calling, caching, context-window management, subagents, background work, debugging, guardrails, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). There are also sections on coding agents, MCP, skills, hooks, model routing, worktree isolation, retries, rate limits, and streaming.

Each chapter follows a practical structure: the problem being addressed, the minimal change needed to solve it, and the trade-offs that come with that change. The book also includes runnable Python code and diagrams to help explain the concepts.

If you're trying to understand what happens behind an AI agent framework, or want to build a basic agent yourself before working with more complex abstractions, this could be a useful resource to explore.

Format: Free online book with source code on GitHub
Language: Python
Topics: AI agents, LLMs, tool calling, context management, MCP, RAG, coding agents
Version: 1.1, October 2026

One of my favorite things about this series has been seeing people share opportunities, communities, and resources that others might not have discovered otherwise.

We've had some really wonderful community finds over the last few weeks, and I honestly can't thank everyone enough for taking the time to find these opportunities, look through them, and send them my way. I know that takes time, and I appreciate every person who thinks of the Radar when they come across something they feel others might find useful 💙

This week, we weren't able to include a community find, but that's completely okay. Hopefully we'll have more wonderful finds from the community as we keep going.

So if you come across an opportunity, fellowship, grant, hackathon, conference, community, resource, or anything else you think more people should know about, please do send it my way. I love seeing what you find, and it helps make this series better for everyone.

A short description alongside the link makes it much easier for me to review and potentially feature it in a future edition.

💙 Reader Updates

I'm looking forward to this section gradually growing over time, and I'd still love to hear from you.

One of my favorite parts of writing Dev Opportunity Radar has been hearing from people who discovered something they otherwise might have missed.

If you discovered an opportunity through the radar, applied to something, joined a community, attended an event, or simply found a resource you hadn't seen before, I'd genuinely love to hear about it.

You don't need to have been accepted or have a big success story to share. Sometimes simply discovering the right opportunity at the right time is already a win.

If you'd like to share an update, feel free to leave a comment on this edition. With your permission, I may feature it in a future 💙 Reader Updates section and tag you so other readers can celebrate your journey too.

I hope this section gradually becomes a place where we can celebrate those stories together, one update at a time.

👋 Until Next Friday

Before I go, I just want to say thank you.

Every week, I spend time searching for opportunities, resources, and communities that I think deserve a little more attention. But one of my favorite parts of this series isn't the research. It's seeing what happens after an edition is published.

Seeing someone discover an opportunity, apply to a program, share a resource, suggest a Community Find, or come back to tell us what they learned reminds me why I started Dev Opportunity Radar in the first place.

The goal has always been simple:

Help people discover opportunities they otherwise might have missed.

Thanks to all of you, it feels like we're doing exactly that.

Whether you've been reading since the very first edition or this is your first time here, thank you for being part of the journey. Every comment, suggestion, and shared opportunity helps make this series better than I could build on my own.

If you ever come across an opportunity, resource, event, community, or anything else you think deserves more attention, I'd love for you to share it in the comments. And if Dev Opportunity Radar helped you discover something exciting, I'd love to hear that too.

Thank you for reading, for sharing, and for helping make this our radar, not just mine.

I'll be back next Friday with more opportunities, resources, and Community Finds.

Until then, take care, and I hope you discover something amazing this week 💙

📌 Basis Fellowship: $50,000 for Selected Fellows

Who it's for: People working on interesting or unconventional projects, including engineers, scientists, founders, operators, and others pursuing work across different fields.

What it's about:

The Basis Fellowship offers $50,000 to selected fellows, along with access to a network of people working across different areas.

Rather than focusing on one particular industry or type of project, the fellowship is interested in people doing a wide range of work. The examples on its website include an electrical setup, a thermoelectric cloud chamber, and a neurostimulation machine. The idea is to bring together people who might be working on very different things but could benefit from finding one another.

The fellowship doesn't require equity, reporting, or restrictions on how the money is spent. Applicants can submit a portfolio and other useful information, and the application asks them to answer the questions honestly.

People from different backgrounds can apply, whether they're engineers, scientists, operators, or working in another field. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis, and an application doesn't expire if someone isn't selected immediately. Applicants can send updates when something new happens.

There's also a nomination option. If someone you nominate is selected, you receive $1,000. The website also mentions a discretionary $3,000 award for a strong submission that isn't selected.

📌 More Than a Hack 2027: Football Analytics Hackathon

Who it's for: Football analysts, data analysts and scientists, software developers, and tech enthusiasts interested in using data and technology to understand football.

What it's about:

More Than a Hack 2027 is a football analytics hackathon organized by Mobile World Capital Barcelona, Barça Innovation Hub, and Metrica Sports. Participants work with real FC Barcelona match data to develop analytical solutions related to the game.

The hackathon has two online challenge stages, followed by an in-person final pitch at Talent Arena 2027 in Barcelona.

The Initial Challenge asks teams to estimate team possession for every frame of a football match using provided automatic tracking data and homography. Participants don't need to build player detection, identification, appearance, or calibration systems from scratch. Submissions are automatically evaluated and ranked.

The top 20 teams advance to the Innovation Challenge. In this stage, teams can explore analytical or tactical questions using a dataset of 10 professional matches. They can experiment with different approaches to analysis, modeling, interpretation, and generating insights, with specialized technical mentoring available.

The top five teams from this stage will be invited to present their projects at Talent Arena 2027 in Barcelona. Travel and accommodation expenses for the final pitch are covered. The listed prizes also include official FC Barcelona shirts, Barça Innovation Hub merchandise, and an exclusive FC Barcelona experience.

Teams must have 3 to 5 members. Teams with fewer than three members won't be eligible for the Innovation Challenge or the Final Pitch.

Registration is open until November 10, 2026. The Initial Challenge is already underway, so anyone interested should review the schedule and registration requirements before joining.

📌 Perplexity Research Fellowship: AI Research Program

Who it's for: Early-career researchers, engineers, and analysts from technical or quantitative disciplines, including fields such as physics, mathematics, cognitive science, and quantitative finance.

What it's about:

The Perplexity Research Fellowship is a full-time research program for early-career talent interested in advancing AI research. Fellows join Perplexity's R&D teams and work on research areas such as multi-agent planning, continual learning, pre-training, and human-AI interaction.

The program has two tracks:

  • Predoctoral Research Fellow: For exceptional early-career talent from technical or quantitative disciplines.
  • Postdoctoral Research Fellow: For researchers who have recently completed a PhD in a technical or quantitative discipline.

The fellowship runs for three months, with opportunities to extend the program or transition into a full-time, research-focused role. Fellows work in person alongside researchers and engineers at one of Perplexity's offices and may contribute to research publications and other research outputs.

I came across this opportunity after its priority consideration deadline had passed, but applications are still being accepted on a rolling basis until positions are filled. The priority deadline was September 30, 2026, so applications submitted now may not receive priority consideration. The November 2026 and January 2027 cohorts are listed as priority start dates, but it's worth checking the application page for current availability.

Harness Engineering 101: A Practical Guide to Building AI Agents

Who it's for: Developers who want to understand how AI agents work, particularly those interested in LLM APIs, tool use, context management, and building coding agents.

What it's about:

Harness Engineering 101 is a free online book by Isuru Wijesiri that explores how to build AI agents from first principles.

It starts with a simple idea: an LLM provides the reasoning, while the harness is the program that manages the conversation, tools, and execution around it.

The book develops this idea across 16 chapters, using a small Python agent of approximately 300 lines as its foundation. Rather than treating agent frameworks as black boxes, it explains the problems that arise when building an agent and the changes needed to address them.

The chapters cover topics such as the agent loop, tool calling, caching, context-window management, subagents, background work, debugging, guardrails, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). There are also sections on coding agents, MCP, skills, hooks, model routing, worktree isolation, retries, rate limits, and streaming.

Each chapter follows a practical structure: the problem being addressed, the minimal change needed to solve it, and the trade-offs that come with that change. The book also includes runnable Python code and diagrams to help explain the concepts.

If you're trying to understand what happens behind an AI agent framework, or want to build a basic agent yourself before working with more complex abstractions, this could be a useful resource to explore.
